flawed_step: Lines 0014-0016: "Moreover, f cannot belong to T1 (otherwise T1 would contain an edge directly connecting VA and VB other than e, which contradicts the fact that removing e disconnects T1)."
counterexample: Take V = {1,2,3}, T1 = {{1,2},{2,3}}, T2 = {{1,2},{1,3}}. Both are trees on V (each connected, 2 = |V|-1 edges, acyclic). Run the proof's own construction with e = {1,2} in T1, so x = 1, y = 2. Deleting e from T1 leaves the edge {2,3} only, giving components A with VA = {1} and B with VB = {2,3}; indeed x = 1 in VA and y = 2 in VB, and e is the unique T1-edge across the cut. Now take the unique T2-path from x = 1 to y = 2: since {1,2} is an edge of T2 and paths in a tree are unique, that path is 1 -- 2, i.e. k = 1, v0 = 1, v1 = 2. The first index j with vj in VB is j = 1, since v0 = 1 in VA and v1 = 2 in VB. So the proof's construction yields f := {v0, v1} = {1,2}, which is exactly e, and e = {1,2} IS an element of T1. Hence the asserted claim "f cannot belong to T1" is false for this instance. The proof's justification breaks precisely here: it only excludes a cut-crossing T1-edge "other than e", and never excludes f = e, which occurs whenever e lies in T2 as well (an even smaller witness: V = {1,2}, T1 = T2 = {{1,2}}, e = {1,2} forces f = e). Note the exchange itself is still fine in this case (T1' = T1 and T2' = T2), so the failure is of the stated step, not of the theorem.
reasoning_summary: Verified in order. Lines 0002-0005 (removing e from tree T1 leaves exactly two components A, B with vertex sets VA, VB partitioning V, and e the unique T1-edge across the cut) are correct. Lines 0006-0013 (unique T2-path from x to y; first index j with v_{j-1} in VA and v_j in VB; f = {v_{j-1}, v_j} is a T2-edge crossing the cut) are correct. The first step that fails is lines 0014-0016, which asserts f is not in T1. The given justification only rules out a cut-crossing T1-edge OTHER THAN e; it does not rule out f = e, and f = e genuinely occurs whenever e is also an edge of T2, because then the unique T2-path from x to y is the single edge e itself. The three-vertex witness above realizes this. For completeness I checked the remainder: lines 0029-0046 (T1' connected, acyclic, |V|-1 edges) and lines 0047-0060 (deleting f separates x from y in T2, so adding e reconnects without creating a cycle) are each correct, and they remain correct in the degenerate case f = e, so the false claim at 0014-0016 is not load-bearing and the theorem itself is true. The defect is a stated conclusion that overshoots what its own argument establishes (it should read: f is not in T1 \ {e}), and under step-by-step verification that step is unjustified and false as written.
